title: Design an investigation of an agricultural practice and soil quality

stimulus.title: Soil organic matter on a university research farm
stimulus.html: A university research farm grows corn on flat fields that have the same soil type. For the last 12 years, some fields have been plowed every spring and others have been farmed with no-till (seeds planted directly into the residue of the last crop). A student notices that the no-till fields seem darker and crumblier. The farm's records for soil organic matter in the top 15 cm of soil are shown in the graph.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Describe the difference in soil organic matter between the two practices shown in the graph after 12 years. Use numbers from the graph.

rubric.point: Uses values from the graph: after 12 years the no-till fields have about 3.8% organic matter and the plowed fields about 2.6%, a difference of about 1.2 percentage points; or no-till rose from 3.0% while plowed fell from 3.0%.
accept: No-till 3.8%, plowed 2.6%
No-till about 1.2 percentage points higher
No-till increased from 3.0 to 3.8% while plowed decreased to 2.6%

parts.sample: After 12 years the no-till fields had about 3.8% soil organic matter and the plowed fields about 2.6%, so the no-till fields had about 1.2 percentage points more. Both started at 3.0%: no-till rose while the plowed fields fell.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt:
The student wants to test, with a controlled experiment, whether adding cover crops (plants such as rye grown over the winter and left on the field in spring) increases soil organic matter in no-till fields.
(i) Identify a testable hypothesis for the experiment.
(ii) Identify the independent variable.
(iii) Identify the dependent variable.
(iv) Describe an appropriate control group and its purpose.

rubric.point: (i) A testable hypothesis with a direction: If cover crops are grown on no-till fields, then soil organic matter will increase (compared with no-till fields without cover crops).
accept: If rye cover crops are planted each winter, soil organic matter will be higher than in fields without them
A question, or "cover crops will affect organic matter", does not earn the point

rubric.point: (ii) The independent variable is whether a cover crop is grown (cover crop or no cover crop).
accept: Presence or absence of a cover crop
Use of cover crops

rubric.point: (iii) The dependent variable is soil organic matter (percent of soil mass in the top 15 cm).
accept: Percent soil organic matter
Organic matter content of the soil
Corn yield or soil color alone does not earn the point

rubric.point: (iv) A control group of no-till fields with no cover crop, otherwise treated the same, as a baseline to compare with so any difference can be linked to the cover crop.
accept: No-till plots without cover crops, used as a comparison
Must give both the group and its purpose

parts.sample: (i) If no-till fields are planted with a rye cover crop each winter, then their soil organic matter will increase more than in no-till fields without a cover crop. (ii) Independent variable: whether a rye cover crop is grown on the field. (iii) Dependent variable: soil organic matter, as a percent of soil mass in the top 15 cm. (iv) Control: no-till plots that get no cover crop but are otherwise treated exactly the same; they give a baseline, so any difference in organic matter can be attributed to the cover crop rather than to weather or time.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Identify one variable that should be held constant in the experiment.

rubric.point: A relevant constant: soil type, the corn variety, fertilizer amount, the tilling practice (all no-till), the sampling depth, the years of the study, or the weather (plots side by side).
accept: Same soil type in every plot
Same fertilizer amount
Same depth of soil samples
Same corn variety
"Same conditions" alone does not earn the point

parts.sample: Every plot should receive the same amount of fertilizer each year (as well as being the same soil type and sampled to the same 15-cm depth).

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: The student plans to use one field with a cover crop and one field without. Describe a change to the design that would make the results more reliable, and explain how it would help.

rubric.point: Replication: use several plots of each treatment (for example, 6 cover-crop plots and 6 control plots, assigned at random), so that differences between individual fields average out and the result is less likely to be due to one unusual field.
accept: More plots per treatment, randomly assigned, so natural differences average out
Repeat over several years so one unusual year does not decide the result
Must give the change and how it helps

parts.sample: Use several plots of each treatment, for example eight cover-crop plots and eight control plots assigned at random across the farm. With replication, natural differences between fields (a wetter corner, a sandier patch) average out, so a difference between the groups is more likely to be caused by the cover crop.

parts.label: e
parts.prompt: Explain why soil organic matter decreased in the plowed fields in the graph.

rubric.point: Plowing mixes air into the soil and breaks it up, so decomposers break down organic matter faster (its carbon is released as carbon dioxide).
accept: Tilling aerates the soil, speeding decomposition of organic matter
Tilling exposes organic matter to microbes and oxygen

rubric.point: Plowing buries or removes the residue cover and leaves soil bare, so topsoil rich in organic matter is lost to erosion (or less residue is added to the surface).
accept: Bare plowed soil erodes, carrying away the organic-rich topsoil
Less residue left on the surface to build organic matter

parts.sample: Plowing turns the soil over and mixes air into it, so decomposers break down the organic matter faster and its carbon leaves as carbon dioxide. Plowing also buries the residue and leaves the surface bare, so wind and rain erode the topsoil, where most of the organic matter is, and less fresh residue stays on top to replace what is lost.

parts.label: f
parts.prompt: Describe one benefit to the farm of higher soil organic matter, and explain how it provides that benefit.

rubric.point: A benefit with its mechanism: organic matter holds water like a sponge, so crops suffer less in dry spells and less irrigation is needed; or it holds nutrients and releases them slowly, so less fertilizer is needed; or it binds soil into crumbs, so the soil resists erosion and lets water soak in.
accept: More water-holding capacity, so crops survive dry periods
Holds nutrients so less fertilizer is needed
Better soil structure, so less erosion and more infiltration
Naming the benefit without how it works does not earn the point

parts.sample: Higher organic matter increases the soil's water-holding capacity: organic matter soaks up and holds water like a sponge, so the corn has water for longer during dry spells and the farm needs less irrigation.
